blocks.text: 1. Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)

blocks.alt: An input layer feeds hidden layers, which feed the output layer

blocks.text: Perceptron, the previous topic, closed with a genuine, mathematically proven limitation: a single Perceptron cannot solve the XOR problem, or any other problem that is not linearly separable. A Multi-Layer Perceptron stacks many Perceptron-like units together specifically to overcome exactly this weakness.

Multiple layers, each one learning on top of the layer before it, can solve problems a single layer genuinely cannot represent at all. This makes the Multi-Layer Perceptron the first genuinely practical, general-purpose neural network architecture, and the direct structural foundation everything else in this course builds on.
2. The Structural Addition

blocks.alt: A perceptron is one layer while an MLP adds hidden layers

blocks.text: A single Perceptron is just one layer, directly mapping its inputs to a single output with no intermediate step. A Multi-Layer Perceptron adds one or more hidden layers in between the input and the output, exactly the hidden layer concept already introduced in the What Is Deep Learning topic.

Each hidden layer transforms its input into a new, learned representation before passing that representation onward to the next layer, building up increasingly useful, increasingly abstract features one layer at a time, rather than trying to solve the entire problem in a single step.
3. Solving XOR

This connects directly back to the exact XOR problem a single Perceptron cannot solve, covered in depth in the previous topic. A hidden layer with just two neurons can learn two separate, considerably simpler decision boundaries, each one individually still just a straight line.

The output layer then combines those two simpler boundaries together, and this combination can represent a genuinely curved, non-linear decision region that a single straight line never could produce on its own. This is the direct, concrete mechanism by which stacking layers overcomes the Perceptron's core limitation.

blocks.text: 4. A Genuinely Crucial Requirement

blocks.alt: A hidden layer needs a nonlinear activation

blocks.text: A genuinely crucial requirement, easy to overlook at first, is that stacking layers with only linear operations and no activation function at all mathematically collapses back into one single, equivalent linear layer, no matter how many layers were actually stacked together.

Adding a non-linear activation function between layers, covered in full depth in the Activation Functions module immediately following this one, genuinely preserves each layer's own separate, distinct contribution, which is exactly what allows a Multi-Layer Perceptron to represent the curved decision boundaries covered in the previous section.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This is a genuinely common point of confusion. Simply adding more layers does not automatically add more representational power, without a non-linear activation function between them, extra layers are mathematically wasted.

blocks.text: 5. Fully Connected Layers

blocks.alt: Every neuron in a layer connects to every neuron in the next

blocks.text: A Multi-Layer Perceptron is typically fully connected, meaning every single neuron in one layer connects to every single neuron in the very next layer, with no connections skipped or omitted.

Each of these connections has its own individually learned weight, meaning the total number of learnable parameters grows quickly as either the number of layers or the number of neurons per layer increases, a genuine practical consideration covered further in the Network Architecture topic later in this module.
6. Depth Versus Width

blocks.alt: Depth means more layers while width means more neurons per layer

blocks.text: Two genuinely separate design choices shape a Multi-Layer Perceptron's overall capacity. Depth refers to how many hidden layers the network actually has, and more depth generally allows the network to learn more abstract, hierarchical patterns, directly echoing the feature hierarchy already covered in the What Is Deep Learning topic.

Width refers to how many neurons sit within each individual layer, and more width generally allows the network to capture more distinct patterns at any single level, without necessarily needing additional depth to do so. Choosing an appropriate balance between depth and width is a genuine, ongoing design decision, covered in more practical depth in the Network Architecture topic ahead.

blocks.text: 7. A Genuine Training Challenge

blocks.alt: Many layers become genuinely harder to train

blocks.text: This connects back to the Perceptron Learning Rule, already covered in the previous topic, which only works correctly for a single layer with a directly observable error at its output. A Multi-Layer Perceptron cannot use that simple rule directly, since a hidden layer's neurons have no direct, observable correct answer of their own to compare against.

Training a Multi-Layer Perceptron instead requires knowing how every single weight, at every single layer, actually contributed to the network's final output error, a genuinely harder problem than the Perceptron's single-layer case. This is solved by backpropagation, covered in its own full, dedicated module later in this course.
8. A Preview of the Universal Approximation Theorem

This connects forward to the Universal Approximation Theorem, the final topic of this very module. A Multi-Layer Perceptron with even just one sufficiently wide hidden layer can, in principle, approximate essentially any continuous function, a genuinely powerful theoretical result covered in full mathematical depth in that upcoming topic.

This theoretical power is precisely why the Multi-Layer Perceptron became, and remains, such a foundational architecture, it is not merely a practical fix for the XOR problem, but a structure with genuine, provable representational power well beyond that one specific example.
9. The Practical Foundation for Everything Ahead

Every specific architecture covered later in this course, Convolutional Neural Networks, Transformers, and considerably more, ultimately extends, or specializes, this exact same fully connected, multi-layer foundation covered throughout this topic.

A CNN adds specialized connectivity patterns suited to image data, and a Transformer adds specialized attention mechanisms suited to sequences, but underneath these specializations, both still rely on layers of weighted sums and non-linear activations, the exact core mechanics a plain Multi-Layer Perceptron already establishes here.
10. When a Plain MLP Is Genuinely the Right Choice

A plain Multi-Layer Perceptron is genuinely the right choice today for structured, tabular data with a modest number of features, often serving as a genuinely strong, simple baseline before reaching for anything more specialized or complex.

For raw images, audio, or long text sequences, specialized architectures, covered in their own dedicated modules considerably later in this course, generally perform considerably better than a plain Multi-Layer Perceptron would, since they are specifically built to exploit the particular structure those data types actually have.
11. Worked Example
The example below trains a Multi-Layer Perceptron directly on the exact XOR problem the single Perceptron could not solve, demonstrating the fix in practice.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

X_xor = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]])
y_xor = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])

mlp = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(4,), activation="relu", max_iter=2000, random_state=42)
mlp.fit(X_xor, y_xor)

predictions = mlp.predict(X_xor)
accuracy = mlp.score(X_xor, y_xor)

print(f"XOR predictions: {predictions}")
print(f"Actual XOR values: {list(y_xor)}")
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}")
print(f"\nHidden layer weights shape: {mlp.coefs_[0].shape} (input features x hidden neurons)")
print("The hidden layer's 4 neurons learn intermediate boundaries, which the output layer combines to solve XOR correctly")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example achieves 100 percent accuracy on XOR, directly demonstrating the fix covered throughout this topic, a single hidden layer with non-linear activation solves what a single Perceptron mathematically cannot.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: A Multi-Layer Perceptron stacks Perceptron-like units together to overcome the single Perceptron's core limitation.
Hidden layers transform their input into new, learned representations before passing it onward.
Combining two simple decision boundaries lets a hidden layer solve XOR, which a single Perceptron cannot.
Stacking layers without a non-linear activation function collapses into one equivalent linear layer.
A Multi-Layer Perceptron is typically fully connected, with every neuron linked to every neuron in the next layer.
Depth (layer count) and width (neurons per layer) are two separate design choices shaping network capacity.
The simple Perceptron Learning Rule does not work for hidden layers; training requires backpropagation instead.
The Universal Approximation Theorem shows even one sufficiently wide hidden layer has genuine theoretical power.
Next up: Neurons, a closer, more detailed look at the individual computational unit every layer is built from.
